# Tables policy

This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure.

There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented.

## Policy for result data

When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning.

This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things.

No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.

## Why the statistics are a definition list

GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read.

The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context.
# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. Persistence overview describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

Corrupt data policy follows the rejection branches in detail. Storage quota notes explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. Storage testing guide extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Rules
The rules specification is a game contract that defines turns, scores and session changes in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A turn reveals two eligible cards. A match adds one pair, while a miss gives you time to remember the faces before both cards turn back.

## Board

- R01 - Support square boards with side lengths `4`, `6`, `8`, `10`, `12`, `14` and `16`. Every face occurs exactly twice. Positions run from zero in row order.

The deal comes from the board code defined in Reproducibility.

## Turn

- R02 - The first valid card activation reveals that card. Activating it again or activating a matched card has no game effect.
- R03 - The next valid activation reveals a different unmatched card. If the two faces match, keep them revealed and add one matched pair immediately.
- R04 - If the faces differ, show both for `800` active milliseconds, then close both together. Ignore all card activation during this interval. Pause the interval while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume.
- R05 - Add one move when the second valid card is revealed. The first reveal and ignored activation add no moves. Matches and misses each cost one move until the count reaches `999999`. At that cap the count stops increasing. Play continues normally, pairs still match and the game still completes. Show the current move count throughout play as `Moves: N`.

For example, revealing two matching cards produces one move and one matched pair. Revealing the same first card twice still leaves one revealed card and zero moves.

## Completion

- R06 - Give one point per matched pair and no other score. Show matched pairs against the board's total pairs throughout play as `Pairs: M/T`, where `M` is matched pairs and `T` is the total. Complete the game when every pair is matched. Show the final moves and elapsed time with a completion banner. Apply the completion motion defined in Visuals.


## Clock

- R07 - Start elapsed time on the first valid reveal. Count active milliseconds while the page is shown. Pause while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume. Stop at completion. Rendering frequency doesn't change the elapsed time. Cap elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds. At the cap, play continues normally and the clock shows the capped time.

Show the clock throughout play as `Time: m:ss`. Round elapsed seconds down, pad seconds to two digits and let minutes continue past 59. For example, 3600000ms shows `Time: 60:00`.

The mismatch interval and elapsed clock use the same active time. Showing the page again continues the interval from its remaining time.

## Session

- R08 - Start with `4` rows and `4` columns unless a saved supported size exists. Remember the last chosen size after reload. A page load starts a fresh deal. Loading a valid board code or snapshot also saves its size as the last chosen size. A failed load keeps the saved size unchanged.
- R09 - New Game creates a fresh seed at the current size. Restart keeps the current board code. Choosing a different size creates a fresh seed at that size. Each action clears the selection, matched pairs, moves and elapsed time.
- R10 - When play completes a game, keep its moves if they beat the saved best for that size. Keep these records after reload. An equal or worse result keeps the existing best. Starting or restarting a game keeps these records. Show the current size's best move count throughout play and after completion as `Best: N`. Before that size has a record, show `Best: none`.
- R11 - Invalid board codes and snapshots show an error and keep the current game. Invalid saved preferences are ignored. If storage is unavailable, play continues without saving.
- R12 - Starting, restarting, replacing or leaving a game invalidates its pending timer updates. An update from an earlier game or turn can't change the current game.

For example, restarting during a mismatch produces the original hidden deal with zero moves. The earlier mismatch timer can't close a card revealed in the restarted game.

Control behavior is defined in Input. Return to Neon Pairs for the full specification.
# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in Rules.

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in Reproducibility. A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in Input.

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in Neon Pairs.
# Input
Input is a set of controls that lets you play Neon Pairs with a pointer, touch or keyboard.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can reveal a card with a tap, then move to its partner with the arrow keys. Every activation uses the same game action, so changing input methods keeps the same turn.

## Activation

The card controls follow these rules:

- I01 - Render each card as a native button. A primary click, a completed tap, Enter and Space activate the card through the same action.
- I03 - Keep the browser's normal context menu on right-click or long-press. Opening that menu doesn't activate a card.
- I04 - Hover and pointer cancellation leave the game state unchanged.

The game decides whether an activation changes a card. See Rules for matches, repeated selections, blocked turns and turn timing.

## Keyboard movement

- I05 - Give the board one remembered tab stop. When Tab enters the board, focus that card. Use the first card before any board focus has been remembered.

- I06 - Move focus with these keys. Movement changes focus without activating a card:

| Key | Focus destination |
| --- | --- |
| ArrowLeft | Previous card in the same row |
| ArrowRight | Next card in the same row |
| ArrowUp | Card in the previous row and same column |
| ArrowDown | Card in the next row and same column |

The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.

- I07 - Stop arrow movement at a board edge. Moving left from the first column keeps focus on the same card.

- I08 - Let native Tab and Shift+Tab leave the board. Moving through the board uses the movement keys instead of adding every card to the page's tab order.

## Focus

The board keeps focus separate from play:

- I09 - Keep matched cards focusable and mark them `aria-disabled="true"`. Their game action follows the matched-card rule in the gameplay document.
- I10 - While a mismatching pair waits to turn back, allow focus movement and block card activation.
- I11 - On initial load, keep the browser's current focus. Loading the game doesn't move focus to the board.
- I12 - After a new deal, Restart or a successful load, reset the board's remembered tab stop to its first card.
- I13 - When a card receives focus, scroll it into view with nearest alignment in the board's scroll area. Give each card a scroll margin of at least 6px, so its complete focus outline stays in view, including mid-board cards.

The session buttons keep their focus as defined in Controls.

## Card names

The button names describe the information available to the player:

- I14 - Name a hidden card by its one-based row, column and closed state. Keep its face SVG and face identifier out of the DOM while it is hidden, including attributes and accessible text.
- I15 - Name a revealed or matched card by its position, face name and state. Use the face names defined in Visuals.

For example, the first hidden button is named "Row 1, column 1, closed". Once revealed, its name includes the face, so a player can remember it without seeing the drawing.

## Announcements

- I16 - Use one polite, atomic live region for turn results and completion. Announce each turn result exactly once. A winning turn has one announcement containing both the match and the win. Consecutive identical results each get their own announcement. Focus movement, clock renders and closing a mismatch don't repeat a result.

Use these turn announcements, where `M` is the matched pair count, `N` is moves and `time` uses R07's display format:

| Event | Announcement |
| --- | --- |
| First match | Pair found. 1 pair matched. |
| Later match | Pair found. M pairs matched. |
| Miss | No match. Cards close after a short pause. |
| Final match | Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time. |

Send the load statuses in Controls through this same live region once per load event. Keep the visible status beside the reproduction controls.

For example, moving across three cards leaves the current announcement unchanged. Resolving the next pair announces that turn's result.

## Screen reader

- I17 - Support a complete 4x4 keyboard game with a screen reader. Find Grid size and New Game by name, enter the board, expose closed positions and revealed faces by name and state, announce one result per turn and make the win, final moves and time available. Leave the board with Tab and start another game. Deliver automated accessibility-tree evidence for this journey. Record the browser and tool versions in the project README and say whether a screen reader was used. If one was used, record its name and version. The user confirms spoken output during acceptance. Spoken confirmation isn't the developer's deliverable.

# Visuals
Visuals is a design specification that defines the layout, colors and card artwork for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card face combines a shape, a marker position and a fill. You can identify a pair from those features even when you can't distinguish its color.

## Layout

- V01 - Use native controls and a CSS Grid board of DOM card buttons with inline SVG artwork. Render the game without canvas. Use no component library.
- V02 - Center the content within a maximum width of 1120px and give it 16px padding. Keep the outer page within the viewport width.
- V03 - Limit the board's scroll area to `70dvh`, capped at 768px tall. Give it 6px padding and allow overflow on both axes inside that area.
- V04 - Make each card square and size it from 44px to 88px according to the available board width. Use a 6px grid gap, a 2px card border and an 8px card radius.
- V05 - Fit the default four-column board within a phone viewport. When a larger board reaches the 44px minimum card size, keep that size and scroll inside the board.

For example, a sixteen-column board needs 794px for its cards and gaps, plus 12px for board padding. On a phone, the board scrolls while the outer page stays within the viewport width.

The 44px minimum is the chosen card target size. It doesn't state that the complete game conforms to an accessibility standard.

## Colors

- V06 - Use these colors for the page and controls:

| Token | Color | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page | `#090B14` | Page background |
| Panel | `#141827` | Board scroll area, reproduction panel and non-card button, select, input and textarea backgrounds |
| Back | `#1B2034` | Hidden card background |
| Face | `#111625` | Revealed card background |
| Text | `#F4F6FF` | Main text |
| Secondary | `#B8BDD2` | Help text, status labels and optional supporting text |
| Border | `#757C9A` | Neutral borders |
| Focus | `#FFFFFF` | Focus outline |

- V07 - Use this ordered palette for card artwork:

| Index | Name | Color |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Cyan | `#63E7FF` |
| 1 | Magenta | `#FF71D6` |
| 2 | Green | `#8BEA7D` |
| 3 | Yellow | `#FFE082` |
| 4 | Orange | `#FFB064` |
| 5 | Violet | `#B49AFF` |
| 6 | Rose | `#FF8296` |
| 7 | Ice | `#D9F3FF` |

## Type and spacing

- V08 - Use the system sans-serif font stack. Set body text to 16px with a 24px line height, the title to 24px and secondary text to 14px. Secondary text means help text, status labels and optional supporting text.

- V09 - Use spacing values of 4px, 6px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px and 32px for positive layout gaps, padding and margins you set. Allow zero resets and automatic centering. Reset browser default margins. Native control internals aren't covered. Card borders, radii, focus outlines, font metrics and SVG coordinates use their own stated values.

## Card faces

- V10 - Generate 128 face identities from integer face IDs `0` through `127`. Calculate each face from these ordered values:

| Part | Calculation | Ordered values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | `id % 8` | Circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, hexagon, plus, chevron |
| Marker | `floor(id / 8) % 8` | Top, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom, bottom-left, left, top-left |
| Fill | `floor(id / 64)` | Solid, outline |
| Color | Palette at marker index | The eight palette colors above |

- V11 - Treat shape, marker and fill as the face identity. Color repeats the marker distinction and doesn't create a separate identity.

- V12 - Draw each face in an SVG with `viewBox="0 0 100 100"`. Center the main shape within `x=25..75` and `y=25..75`. Draw the marker above the shape as a circle with radius 5, centered 40 units from `(50, 50)` in its marker direction. Give the marker a 3-unit stroke in the Face background color, so it stays separate from the shape. Normalize diagonal directions, giving offsets of about 28.284 units on each axis. Use a 5-unit stroke for an outlined shape. At 44px, all 128 identities must be distinguishable in a grayscale face sheet, including solid and outlined squares with diagonal markers.

Use the face color for the solid shape's fill, the outlined shape's stroke and the marker's fill. An outlined shape has no fill. The marker keeps its Face-background stroke.

- V13 - Name each face with lowercase palette, fill, shape and marker names in the form "{color} {fill} {shape}, marker {position}". For example, face `0` is "cyan solid circle, marker top". Face `64` is "cyan outline circle, marker top".

## Card states

- V14 - Give every hidden card the same back with a neutral diamond. Hidden cards keep their face artwork out of the DOM, as Input requires.
- V15 - Show the face artwork on revealed cards. Keep it shown on matched cards and add a Green palette border and check mark. Keep matched cards at full opacity.
- V16 - Show keyboard focus with a 3px white outline offset by 2px. Hover changes only the border to the Text color. Matched cards keep their Green border when hovered.
- V17 - Use a 120ms border-color transition. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, turn that transition off.

The gameplay document defines when card states change. See Rules for turn timing and completion.

## Completion

- V18 - Show a win banner when the game finishes. Give it one 600ms pulse, then keep the banner static. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, show the static banner immediately. Use neither flashing nor confetti.

## Large boards

- V19 - At viewport sizes 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS pixels, render all 256 cards of a 16x16 board. Keep the page within the viewport width and keep controls reachable. Keep each card at least 44px square, with scrolling confined to the board when needed. Reach the first and last card by touch scrolling and by keyboard. Scroll focused cards fully into view without clipping their focus outline.

## Browser zoom

- V20 - At a 640x400 CSS-pixel viewport with device scale 2, the equivalent layout of 200% browser zoom from 1280x800, keep controls, status and the win summary readable without overlap. Keep the page within the viewport width. Keep both a 4x4 board and a 16x16 board playable with pointer and keyboard. Allow board scrolling and keep the focused card and its complete focus outline in view. Don't disable pinch zoom.

# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. Clock design discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. Mismatch interval covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. Elapsed time rules covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. Clock design follows those cases in detail, and Test policy explains the runners.

# Test strategy
This page explains how Neon Pairs divides evidence between game tests, browser journeys, source checks and user acceptance.

The product contract is specification version 2.2. The README records a successful named compatibility run. Known issues tracks verification limits, and Fixtures explains why replacing reviewed JSON expectations with current output would weaken the evidence.

## Start with the question

A deck test asks whether a code produces the published cards. A browser test asks whether a player can reach and activate those cards through rendered controls. An accessibility-tree capture asks what Chromium exposes to assistive software. None can substitute for the others.

The useful division follows the architecture's existing boundaries:

| Question | Existing evidence | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does a turn change the right data? | Vitest tests beside `game.ts` | Native focus, scrolling or pointer dispatch |
| Does the seeded deal match the format? | Literal vectors and `tests/deal-oracle.ts` | Whether hidden identities leak into markup |
| Does the browser adapter count active time? | Pure clock tests plus controlled browser clocks | Real device scheduling latency |
| Can a player finish through the interface? | Built-page keyboard and touch journeys | Spoken screen-reader output |
| Does local storage survive reload? | HTTP-origin persistence journeys | Cross-browser behavior of disk-origin storage |
| Does the distribution stand alone? | Offline disk navigation and built-output inspection | Every browser engine or operating system |
| Does the layout survive difficult geometry? | Large-board, scrollbar, zoom and focus tests | Every possible window size |

This is a map of current checks, not a demand to create one test of each kind for every change. A correction to snapshot validation usually needs parser evidence first. A clipped focus ring needs browser geometry. A change to explanatory copy may need only the relevant reviewed expectation and a visual check. Unit tests and Browser tests show the local conventions.

## Pure behavior carries the broad matrix

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. The package's `test` script is `vitest run`. Most of these tests import `test` from Vitest and assertions from `node:assert/strict`. They do not mount React to prove a card transition.

The core state includes the immutable board description, its deck, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the started flag. Selection has closed, one-card and mismatch branches. Tests exercise transitions directly, allowing exact questions such as whether advancing a pending miss by 799ms leaves it open and whether the next millisecond closes both cards.

The suite checks complete pairs at all seven supported sizes. `completion.test.ts` finishes each size through `activateCard`; it does not infer that a 4x4 success proves a 16x16 finish. `deck.test.ts` checks the published seed-one vector, generator states, the inclusive maximum seed, frozen data and independent generation at each size. `deck-rejection.test.ts` targets uncommon rejection-sampling boundaries using separately stored expected decks.

The game tests also make negative cases visible. A fractional or out-of-range card index returns the old state. Repeating the first selected card adds no move. During a miss, every activation is ignored. Invalid elapsed steps leave the game unchanged. Keeping the original object in those cases is observable behavior in these tests; asserting identity can distinguish an ignored action from an unnecessary reconstruction.

Snapshot and replay tests carry a different matrix: exact object fields, integer ranges, byte limits, valid selections and action ordering. A round trip is useful, but two matching mistakes can round trip successfully. Independent expected fields and malformed inputs provide the stronger evidence. A valid started game with one revealed card and zero moves is the baseline for several invalid-counter cases, so rejection can be attributed to the changed counter rather than an unrelated invalid state.

## Session tests connect results to browser-independent policy

`src/game/session/session.ts` is a data adapter. Its tests create sessions and call `activateSession`, `replaceGame` and `tickSession` directly. This makes several integration rules cheap to check without pretending to test browser effects.

A replacement increments `generation`. A tick carrying an earlier generation has no effect. An unfinished imported game is paused and cannot accept card input or active time until resumed. A locally completed game can improve the appropriate saved move record. A completed import follows the import path instead of the live completion path. These are separate causes even when both render a completed board.

Session feedback tests inspect event progression as well as text. Two misses with the same wording still represent two turns. Focus movement and time advancement do not represent new turn results. Browser announcement tests then verify that these data changes become the intended DOM updates. Checking both layers helps distinguish a missing session event from a rendering problem.

Storage tests use the narrow `PreferenceStore` interface. A Map-backed implementation covers round trips and per-size minima; a throwing implementation covers failures without a browser. Browser tests separately exercise a denied `window.localStorage` getter. The distinction matters because failure while obtaining the store occurs before either `getItem` or `setItem` can run.

## Browser journeys use the shipped shape

The package's `test:e2e` command runs the main build, builds diagnostic entries, and then invokes Node's test runner over `tests/*.e2e.test.ts` with concurrency set to one. Playwright drives Chromium, while `node:test` owns the tests. There is no Playwright Test project configuration controlling this suite's retry or worker behavior.

Most journey files import the wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts`. It launches a browser, creates a fresh context per case, collects page errors and closes resources. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the freshly built HTML on a private loopback port. `GAME_URL` points at the same build on disk. Persistence journeys use the served URL; offline-delivery checks use the disk URL.

Fresh contexts isolate browser storage, permissions and page-installed instrumentation. They do not make every global resource independent: the artifact server and browser belong to file-level hooks, and the runtime record has a shared output location. The serial command is part of the implementation being documented. Flaky-test notes discuss the timing consequences.

The browser tests use public controls to load `np1-4-1`. They know its deck from the documented format and test fixture, rather than asking the application for hidden state. The board's hidden buttons expose positions and closed state. The tests inspect that absence directly in `input-contract.e2e.test.ts`, including the neutral back and lack of face artwork. A solver that depended on hidden SVGs would invalidate this evidence.

## Contract checks complement shared labels

Ordinary journey helpers import the control-label constants so they can focus on behavior. Contract tests also contain literal labels and limits. This prevents changing a production constant and every test lookup together from silently changing the public contract.

`control-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers native reproduction controls, their input limits, invalid statuses and action focus. `product-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers status presentation, continuing minutes and successful load size selection. `persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks record comparisons, saved sizes and fresh progress after reload. These overlap broader journeys at specific seams, where a shared helper could otherwise conceal a mistake.

Overlap is useful when the assertions answer different questions. Loading a snapshot appears in parser tests, session tests and browser tests because validation, paused data and Resume focus are different behaviors. Repeating the same serializer implementation as an expected-value helper would add little protection. The suite's independent literal expectations are intended to break that circularity.

## Visual and accessibility evidence are concrete

The art entry renders every face at the minimum card size. Tests capture color, grayscale and neutral versions. Neutral silhouettes are compared for uniqueness, and separate assertions inspect marker geometry and palette application. This establishes machine-distinguishable geometry; a person still reviews whether the distinctions are usable. Accessibility audit explains that limit.

Layout tests inspect page width, card bounds, board scrolling and complete focus outlines. The large-board checks cover 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS-pixel viewports. A separate equivalent-zoom journey uses 640x400 with device scale 2. Visible-scrollbar cases remove Chromium's default scrollbar-hiding launch argument and test widths where scrollbar space changes the available board area.

The accessibility journey uses the Chromium DevTools Protocol to capture the accessibility tree during a complete keyboard game. It checks controls, revealed and matched names, disabled state exposure, results, completion, Tab exit and a fresh game. The artifact records browser and Playwright versions and explicitly records that a screen reader was not run. User acceptance owns the spoken journey. Tree assertions support that review; they do not prove speech delivery.

## Source and delivery checks

`source-audit.test.ts` inspects package pins, lockfile agreement, compiler settings and source conventions required by the architecture and technology specifications. It reads authored files rather than the compiled bundle. `source-conventions.test.ts` checks current export ownership, question-shaped predicate names, behavior-oriented test names and the small set of environment reads the runners use.

These are text checks with intentionally limited reach. The core effect scan names particular source files. It is not an analysis of every transitive call. The TypeScript source scan can reject spelling patterns, but cannot prove full semantic purity. Review remains necessary when moving behavior to a new module. Code review and Source audit notes provide related architectural context.

The built-output test searches the emitted HTML for `fetch(` and the preload helper's `relList` marker. The offline journey blocks network access and checks that only the document request occurs while a card remains playable. Together they cover bundle content and observed loading. Neither measures first-render duration; Performance budget documents that evidence gap.

## Following through

Choose the smallest test that exposes the changed behavior, then follow it into the browser where native interaction or effects matter. Regression catalogue shows paired investigations, and Release checklist assembles the complete verification sequence. The remaining evidence gaps are tracked in Known issues.
# ADR 055: Review behavior and evidence together

This record explains the rationale for reviewing behavior and evidence before integration.

## Decision context

The project uses small modules, strict typing and several layers of tests, but none of those tools independently decides whether a change expresses the intended game behavior. A parser can be well typed and accept the wrong fields. A timer can be thoroughly tested and still use a mistaken definition of active time. Review connects the stated behavior to the implementation and its evidence.

The workflow discussion favored review before integrating a change so that behavior, implementation and evidence could be assessed together.

## What a reviewer can assess

A useful change description starts with the trigger and resulting behavior. For a mismatch fix, the reviewer needs to know whether the problem occurred at an exact closing edge, after visibility changed or after replacing a deal. Those are different risks even if all involve a timer.

The source then makes the mechanism inspectable. Pure transitions live in `game.ts`; browser observation and lifecycle live in the session hooks; focus and scrolling live in the board. A change that crosses those boundaries deserves an explanation of why each piece moves. Architecture supplies that shared vocabulary.

Evidence follows the claim. A literal deck vector supports generation stability. A parser test supports rejection of an inconsistent snapshot. A browser journey supports the focus result after Resume. A screenshot supports an artwork observation. Review is stronger when the evidence matches the behavior than when a long list of unrelated commands is attached.

## An example review path

Consider changing the clock so a late callback closes a mismatch correctly. The reviewer can inspect whether measured deltas remain fractional, whether the current generation is checked and whether synchronization still happens before activation. Focused clock tests can exercise arithmetic; browser edge tests can show the adapter's effect.

A broad refactor that merely moves code has a different burden: the reviewer looks for preserved boundaries, unchanged format constants and stable imported behavior. A formatting-only change has less semantic surface. Scaling explanation to the actual change keeps the process useful rather than ceremonial.

## Alternatives and costs

Relying solely on a green suite would make untested assumptions easy to integrate. Requiring human review to manually repeat every automated check would waste time and still be less precise at numeric edges. The chosen rationale gives tools the repeatable assertions and people the interpretation, scope and maintainability questions.

Review adds latency, especially when the change is small. Small behavior files and focused descriptions reduce that cost by making the result understandable. The point is not to expand every fix into a design process; it is to keep the relationship between problem, code and proof visible.

## Historical and current evidence

The repository contains source audits, exact-version checks and a README verification record. Those are concrete aids to review.

Code review guide, ADR 052, ADR 053 and ADR 054 are the neighboring pages. The practical outcome is a reviewable implementation with proportionate evidence.

docs/motion-policy.md:18:Both component stylesheets contain a `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media query. The card query sets `transition: none`; the status query sets `animation: none` on `.celebrate`. Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, new elements run no animation and no transition. This keeps the static visual states available immediately when the preference is active. The existing cards still change their border and artwork when their state changes; the change simply has no interpolated border effect.
docs/motion-policy.md:42:The flag can remain true after the CSS animation has finished. That does not make the effect repeat on every timer update: an existing element retaining the same animation class is different from mounting a new element or changing its animation name. The final game also stops advancing its active elapsed time. The relevant session behavior is covered more fully in Session module.
docs/tables-policy.md:13:No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format.
docs/tables-policy.md:37:The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.
docs/tables-policy.md:47:Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.
docs/randomness-policy.md:5:A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. Deck generation covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration.
docs/randomness-policy.md:9:`src/game/session/fresh-board.ts` exports `freshBoardCode(size, previousSeed?)`. It obtains a seed and returns the normal board-code representation through `boardCode` from `deck.ts`. Only src/game/session/fresh-board.ts may call a random source. Everything else that needs randomness imports it from there. The session controller uses that exported operation when initializing a session or asking for a new game.
docs/randomness-policy.md:25:When `previousSeed` is supplied, a candidate equal to it is discarded. `use-game.ts` passes the current game's seed when creating a new game, including when a different grid size is selected. This means the next seed differs from the immediately preceding seed even across a size change.
docs/randomness-policy.md:64:## Every action that chooses or reuses a deal
docs/randomness-policy.md:76:This table is useful when a bug report says that “a new board changed.” A new game is expected to change the seed. A restart or imported code is expected to repeat the existing deal. A size selection is a fresh deal rather than a geometric rearrangement of the old cards.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:3:This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:9:For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:11:The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:53:A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:55:Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.
docs/storage-failure-policy.md:73:These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. Storage testing guide extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.
docs/test-policy.md:9:The core has adjacent tests such as `game.test.ts`, `deck.test.ts`, `snapshot.test.ts` and `replay.test.ts`. Their names make the behavior under discussion easy to locate before reading the whole suite. A feature's rules.ts has a rules.test.ts beside it. Complete interaction journeys remain at the application test level, where focus, storage, browser lifecycle and delivery can be observed together.
docs/test-policy.md:41:Snapshot tests check outer keys, numeric bounds, matched-position consistency and each selection form. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` focuses on nested selection invariants. A selected index must name an available position, a mismatch must involve different faces and complete matched pairs must be represented together. The decoder reconstructs its deck from the code before checking these relationships.
docs/test-policy.md:57:The browser wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts` creates a new context per journey and registers its closure with the Node test context. It collects page errors and asserts that none occurred after a successful journey body. It creates an artifact directory from the test name and restricts output paths to a filename. A shared browser and local server are closed in the file-level teardown.
docs/time-policy.md:9:`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.
docs/time-policy.md:21:An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.
docs/time-policy.md:27:`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.
docs/time-policy.md:33:A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. Clock design discusses this small function and the hook separately.
docs/time-policy.md:37:`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.
docs/time-policy.md:45:The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.
docs/time-policy.md:55:A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.
docs/time-policy.md:57:The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.
docs/time-policy.md:71:Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:9:A name can arrive with incidental spaces from typing, pasting or an input method. Keeping several representations of that same entered name would make later display and comparison harder to reason about. Every name a person types is stored and shown after trimming both ends, collapsing each run of inner whitespace to one space and normalizing to NFC. The stored value and visible value therefore describe the same processed name rather than exposing the original draft in one view and a different spelling in another.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:37:That distinction leaves room to implement an editing experience without confusing it with persistence. A reviewer can inspect where a completed entry crosses from local draft state into the feature's model and where the model is rendered. If display uses an old raw draft while storage uses the processed value, the two surfaces no longer have the relationship described above.
docs/text-entry-policy.md:79:The current code's strongest relevant lesson is explicit boundaries: BoardCodeForm submits a draft, the controller validates, replacement updates the model, and rendered controls follow that model. Names need their own representation boundary within the feature that introduces them. The present board-code and snapshot controls use their own input boundaries.
docs/target-size-policy.md:9:The existing code already gives cards a minimum track size and shared controls a minimum height. Extending the interface calls for checking the actual rendered target in the phone layout, where flex wrapping and available width matter. Every new control is at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels at a 390 pixel wide viewport. This policy covers the rendered control area rather than enlarging only a decorative child or a focus ring.
docs/target-size-policy.md:11:The current styles are useful building blocks, but they are not proof of every dimension for an arbitrary new element. In particular, `.control` declares minimum height without a general minimum width. A new short-label action could be tall enough while still being too narrow. The policy check and the existing class definition therefore answer related but different questions.
docs/target-size-policy.md:45:A visual review at a wide desktop window can miss the consequences of a new wrapper or label. Selectors such as `.controls > button` and `.control-row > button` apply to direct children. If a wrapper changes which element grows, measuring the wrapper rather than the actual button can hide a target-width problem.
docs/target-size-policy.md:73:For a new feature review, a concise measurement record can identify the viewport, the control's role and name, its width and height and whether it is fully reachable. The record is most useful alongside the rendered layout, because it can reveal that a formally large button is covered by another element or forced beyond the page edge. This is observation of the target in context, not a second numerical policy.
